title: There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who look spiritually alive… but inwardly, they are exhausted.
paragraphs: There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who look spiritually alive… but inwardly, they are exhausted.
Not because they stopped loving Jesus.
But because somewhere along the way, they confused serving Christ with sitting at His feet.
And the terrifying part is this…
Martha never stopped believing in Jesus.
She simply became too distracted to enjoy Him.
That is why the story of Martha and Mary is one of the most misunderstood and emotionally dangerous passages in the entire Bible.
Because this story is not merely about two sisters.
It is about two kinds of Christians.
And if we are honest…
both women are living inside many of us at the exact same time.
In Luke 10:38–42, Scripture says:
“Now it happened as they went that He entered a certain village; and a certain woman named Martha welcomed Him into her house.”
At first glance, Martha appears admirable.
Responsible.
Faithful.
Productive.
Dependable.
The type every church depends on.
The Greek word used in Luke 10:40 says Martha was:
“περιεσπᾶτο” (periespato)

Meaning:
“dragged away,”
“pulled apart,”
“distracted in many directions.”
This is far deeper than being “busy.”
The word paints the image of a soul being internally torn apart.
Martha was not simply cooking dinner.
Her spirit was being violently fragmented.
And this is where modern Christianity quietly breaks people.
Because many believers are applauded for spiritual productivity while their intimacy with Christ is slowly dying in silence.
Martha welcomed Jesus into the house…
but Mary welcomed Jesus into her heart.
That distinction changes everything.
Luke writes:
The phrase “sat at His feet” in Jewish culture carried massive spiritual meaning.
This was the posture of a disciple.
In Acts 22:3, Paul says he was educated “at the feet of Gamaliel.”

To sit at someone’s feet meant:
“I surrender to your authority.”
“I want your wisdom.”
“I belong to your teaching.”
Mary was not being lazy.
Mary chose devotion over performance.
And religion hates that.
Because religious systems often reward visible labor more than hidden intimacy.
But heaven does not measure faithfulness the way crowds do.
Then comes one of the most emotionally revealing moments in Scripture.
Martha finally explodes.
“Lord, do You not care…?”
That sentence exposes the human heart.
People overwhelmed by serving eventually begin questioning the love of God.
That still happens today.

People pray:
“Lord, do You not care that I’m carrying this family?”
“Do You not care that I’m burned out?”
“Do You not care that I’m doing everything alone?”
Martha’s frustration was not ultimately with Mary.
It was with God.
Busyness had distorted her perception of Jesus.
And then Christ responds with heartbreaking tenderness.
“Martha, Martha…”
Whenever names are repeated in Scripture, it signals deep emotion.

“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Samuel, Samuel.”
“Saul, Saul.”
Jesus was not rebuking her with cruelty.
He was grieving for her.
Then He says:
“You are anxious and troubled about many things.”
The Greek words here are devastatingly revealing.

“μεριμνᾷς” (merimnas)
means:
to be mentally pulled apart by anxiety.

“θορυβάζῃ” (thorybazē)
means:
inner turmoil,
noise,
restlessness,
emotional disturbance.
Martha’s problem was never cooking.
Her problem was internal noise.
And that describes countless Christians today.
Always active.
Always posting.
Always serving.
Always doing ministry.
Yet spiritually starving.
Some people know church culture better than they know the voice of God.
That sentence hurts because many of us recognize ourselves inside it.
Then Jesus says something revolutionary:
“But one thing is necessary.”
The Greek says:

“ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία”
(Henos de estin chreia)
“Only one thing is truly needed.”
Not ten things.
Not endless striving.
Not spiritual image management.
One thing.
Presence with Him.
And then comes the line that destroys the performance-based mindset of modern Christianity:
“Mary has chosen the good portion.”
The phrase “good portion” echoes Psalm 16:5:
“The LORD is the portion of my inheritance.”
Mary chose Christ Himself as her inheritance.
Not activity.
Not appearance.
Not reputation.
Jesus was enough.
This is the untold truth most people miss:
Martha represents Christians who know how to work for Jesus.
Mary represents Christians who know how to love Jesus.
And many churches unconsciously produce Marthas faster than Marys.
We train people to lead before teaching them to linger.
To perform before they learn surrender.
To preach before they learn silence.
To serve before they learn worship.
And eventually souls collapse under the weight of religious performance.
Because activity without intimacy always becomes exhausting.
But intimacy with Christ transforms obedience into delight.
The shocking part is this:
Martha was close to Jesus physically…
while remaining emotionally distant internally.
That still happens every Sunday.
People can sing worship songs while their hearts are miles away.
They can quote Scripture while privately feeling numb.
They can lead ministries while secretly feeling spiritually dead.
Outward closeness does not guarantee inward communion.
Mary understood something Martha did not yet understand:
Jesus did not come merely to be used.
He came to be loved.
And here is the part almost nobody talks about…
Martha eventually changed.
In John 11, after Lazarus dies, Martha runs to Jesus again.
But this time something is different.
She says:
“Yes, Lord; I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God…”
Pain transformed her theology into surrender.
Sometimes heartbreak becomes the doorway into deeper intimacy with Christ.
Some of you reading this have spent years being Martha.

Serving.
Carrying.
Fixing.
Managing.
Performing.
Pretending you’re spiritually okay.

But inwardly…
you are tired in places nobody sees.
And Jesus is not asking you to abandon responsibility.
He is asking you to stop trying to earn closeness with Him through constant striving.
Because salvation was never built on your performance.
The Hebrew concept of rest throughout Scripture is deeply connected to trust.
The word “שָׁלוֹם” (shalom) does not merely mean peace.

It means:
wholeness,
completeness,
nothing missing,
nothing broken.
Mary found shalom at the feet of Christ.
Martha found fragmentation inside distraction.
And many believers today are collapsing emotionally because they are trying to carry burdens Jesus never asked them to carry.
You do not have to become spiritually famous to be deeply loved by God.
You do not have to constantly prove your worth to heaven.

Jesus never said:
“Come to Me all who are productive.”
He said:
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
The Greek word for “rest” there is:
“ἀναπαύσω” (anapausō)

Meaning:
to refresh,
to revive,
to give calm strength again.
Not temporary escape.
Deep restoration.
And maybe that is why this story survives across centuries.
Because every generation creates more Marthas.
Anxious believers.
Exhausted disciples.
Overstimulated Christians trying to earn what Jesus already purchased at the cross.
But heaven still honors Marys.

People who know how to stop.
Listen.
Weep.
Worship.
Remain.
People who choose presence over applause.
The frightening reality is this:
A Christian can spend years working in God’s house while neglecting God Himself.
And eventually the soul notices the difference.
Be honest…
When was the last time you sat with Jesus without rushing?
Without multitasking?
Without checking notifications every few minutes?
Without turning prayer into a performance?
Without secretly measuring your spiritual worth by productivity?
This story was never meant to shame hardworking believers.
It was meant to rescue them.
Because Jesus loved Martha too much to leave her trapped inside anxious striving.
And He loves you too much to leave you there either.
And if you know someone silently drowning beneath pressure, burnout, anxiety, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them today.
Some people are not losing faith…
they are losing intimacy.
And never forget this:
Some people are busy serving God while starving for God.
